title: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.14 Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
intro: After this lesson you can decide between a chi-square test for independence and for homogeneity, write the hypotheses in context, check the three conditions including expected counts, and name the test.

moments.title: When to use chi-square
moments.text: Categorical variables only, shown as counts in a two-way table. Observed counts are compared with expected counts.

moments.title: Test for independence
moments.text: One sample from one population, two categorical variables. Is there an association?

moments.title: Test for homogeneity
moments.text: Two or more populations or groups, one categorical variable. Are the distributions the same?

moments.title: Grade level and favorite subject
moments.text: One sample of students, two variables measured on each student. Independence.

moments.title: Public, private and charter schools
moments.text: Separate samples from three school types, one variable. Homogeneity.

moments.title: Homework format and grade level
moments.text: A two-way table of counts for one sample. Independence.

moments.title: Observed against expected
moments.text: The test compares observed counts with the counts expected if there were no association.

moments.title: Gym members: age and workout type
moments.text: One random sample, two variables. Independence.

moments.title: Seven steps
moments.text: Name, parameter, hypotheses, conditions, test statistic, p-value, conclusion. This topic covers the first four.

moments.title: Define the premise in context
moments.text: Name the population and the categorical variables, or the populations and the one variable.

moments.title: Independence hypotheses
moments.text: $H_0$: no association between the variables in the population. $H_a$: there is an association.

moments.title: Homogeneity hypotheses
moments.text: $H_0$: the distribution is the same across the populations. $H_a$: the distributions differ.

moments.title: Randomization condition
moments.text: Independence needs a random sample. Homogeneity needs independent random samples or a randomized experiment.

moments.title: Expected counts condition
moments.text: Every expected count is at least 5. Check expected counts, not observed counts.

moments.title: Typical mistakes
moments.text: Mixing up independence and homogeneity, using generic hypotheses, and skipping the conditions.

cards.name: Independence
cards.text: One sample from one population. Two categorical variables. Question: are they associated?

cards.name: Homogeneity
cards.text: Separate samples from two or more populations (or treatment groups). One categorical variable. Question: are the distributions the same?

cells: One sample of students, each asked grade level and favorite subject
Samples from public, private and charter schools, each asked favorite subject
Pet owners sampled in each of three cities, each asked the type of pet
One random sample of gym members asked age group and workout type
Volunteers randomly assigned to three diets, then classified as improved or not
A random sample of adults asked favorite color and favorite cereal

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Decide from how the data were collected, not from the question wording. Separate samples or treatment groups mean homogeneity; one sample with two variables means independence.

questions.obj: Set up a chi-square test for independence
questions.q: A gym surveyed a random sample of 200 members and recorded each member's age group (under 30, 30 to 50, over 50) and preferred workout type (cardio, weights, group classes). The row totals are 70, 90, and 40, and the column totals are 70, 60, and 70. Set up a test of whether age group and preferred workout type are associated.

steps.t: Name the test and the parameter in context.

work.text: This is a chi-square test for independence between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym. One random sample was classified by two categorical variables.
$H_0$: there is no association between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym. $H_a$: there is an association between them.

steps.t: Assumptions: check randomization and the 10% condition.

work.text: The sample is random, and 200 members are less than 10% of all members of a gym.

steps.t: Assumptions: check that every expected count is at least 5, starting with the smallest.

work.text: Expected counts, not observed counts, must be at least 5. This is the smallest of the nine, so all nine are at least 5.

questions.answer: A chi-square test for independence is appropriate. $H_0$: there is no association between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym. $H_a$: there is an association between them. The sample is random, 200 is less than 10% of all members, and every expected count is at least 5.

questions.obj: Set up a chi-square test for homogeneity
questions.q: Researchers took a random sample of pet owners from each of three cities: 90 from City A, 80 from City B, and 80 from City C. Each owner reported owning a cat, a dog, or another pet. The column totals are 75 cat owners, 95 dog owners, and 80 owners of another pet. Set up a test of whether the distribution of pet type is the same in all three cities.

steps.t: Name the test and the parameter in context.

work.text: This is a chi-square test for homogeneity of the distribution of pet type across the three cities for all pet owners in those cities. There are three separate samples and one categorical variable.
$H_0$: the distribution of pet type is the same across the three cities for all pet owners. $H_a$: the distribution of pet type is different for at least one city.

steps.t: Assumptions: check randomization and the 10% condition for each sample.

work.text: Each city's sample is random, and each is less than 10% of the pet owners in its city. Check the condition three times.

steps.t: Assumptions: check that every expected count is at least 5, starting with the smallest.

work.text: Expected counts, not observed counts, must be at least 5. This is the smallest of the nine, so all nine are at least 5.

questions.answer: A chi-square test for homogeneity is appropriate. $H_0$: the distribution of pet type is the same across the three cities for all pet owners. $H_a$: the distribution is different. The samples are random, each is less than 10% of its city's pet owners, and every expected count is at least 5.

traps.title: Independence hypotheses in context
traps.weak: $H_0$: the variables are independent. $H_a$: they are not.
traps.better: $H_0$: there is no association between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym. $H_a$: there is an association between age group and preferred workout type for all members of the gym.

traps.title: Homogeneity hypotheses in context
traps.better: $H_0$: the distribution of favorite subject is the same for public, private and charter school students in the state. $H_a$: the distribution of favorite subject is different for at least one type of school.

traps.title: Checking observed counts instead of expected
traps.weak: Every count in the table is at least 5, so the condition is met.
traps.better: Compute the expected counts from the totals and check that every expected count is at least 5.

traps.title: Using homogeneity language for one sample
traps.weak: Test whether the distribution of workout type is the same across age groups, from one sample of members.
traps.better: There is one random sample with two variables, so this is a test for independence: is there an association between age group and workout type?

traps.title: Writing parameters with sample symbols
traps.better: Hypotheses refer to the population or populations, in words in context, not to sample statistics.

questions.stem: A librarian randomly selects 100 students in each of Grades 9, 10 and 11 and asks each whether they prefer print or e-books. Which test is appropriate?
why: There are three separate samples, not one sample with two variables.
Correct. Independent samples from three populations and one categorical variable: homogeneity.
More than two groups require chi-square, not a two-sample $z$ test.
There is more than one sample.

questions.stem: Which pair of hypotheses is correct for a chi-square test for independence on library data: one random sample of 300 students, classified by grade and by print or e-book preference?
opts: $H_0$: the distribution of format is the same in all grades; $H_a$: it differs
$H_0$: grade and format are not associated; $H_a$: they are associated
why: Hypotheses are never about sample statistics.
Correct. Independence hypotheses are about association between two variables in one population.
This is a hypothesis about proportions, not association in a two-way table.

questions.stem: A table has row totals 60, 60, 60 and column totals 90 and 90 with a grand total of 180. What is the expected count for the cell in row 1, column 1?
why: This is the row proportion, not a count.
Adding the totals does not give an expected count.
Dividing a column total by the number of rows ignores the row total.

questions.stem: Which is part of the conditions for a chi-square test for independence?
opts: Every observed count is at least 5.
The two samples have equal sizes.
why: Correct. A random sample is the randomization condition.
The condition is about expected counts, not observed counts.
Equal sample sizes are not required.
Chi-square tests are for categorical data; there is no normality condition.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A health department randomly selected 50 patients at Clinic A, 50 at Clinic B and 40 at Clinic C, and recorded whether each improved or stayed the same after a flu program. The counts (improved, stayed the same) were: Clinic A 34 and 16, Clinic B 27 and 23, Clinic C 19 and 21.
parts: (a) Which chi-square test is appropriate? Justify.
sample: (a) Chi-square test for homogeneity, because there are separate samples from three clinics and one categorical variable.
(b) $H_0$: the distribution of outcome (improved or stayed the same) is the same for all patients at the three clinics. $H_a$: the distribution of outcome differs for at least one clinic.
(c) Row totals 50, 50, 40; column totals 80, 60; total 140. Improved: A 28.6, B 28.6, C 22.9. Stayed the same: A 21.4, B 21.4, C 17.1.
(d) Independent random samples. Each sample is less than 10% of the patients at its clinic. All expected counts are at least 5 (the smallest is 17.1).
checklist: (b) Null: same distribution across the clinics, in context
(c) Row total times column total over grand total

flags.text: The CED expected-counts condition says "greater than 5"; the video says "five or greater". The page says "at least 5", which matches common AP scoring.

The CED description of chi-square distributions (nonnegative, skewed right, skew lessens with degrees of freedom) is not covered in the video. It appears once in the Method section without a video link.
